nodes.header: Time Management & Productivity
Pomodoro Technique
nodes.body: Stage 1 — Draft. A focus method that alternates short work intervals with breaks to avoid burnout during studying or extended work sessions. Adopted by Jolene in her studies. Standard configuration is 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute break (one Pomodoro). Pitfalls and validation pending more episodes.

nodes.header: Pitfalls: Pomodoro Technique
Eisenhower Matrix
nodes.body: Stage 1 — Draft. A prioritization framework that sorts tasks into four boxes by urgency and importance, helping users decide what to do, schedule, delegate, or drop when overwhelmed. Used by Deborah and recommended by her to Jolene on 2023-03-22 as a method for staying focused under heavy load. The visual breakdown (a 2x2 grid) is part of how Deborah teaches it.

nodes.header: Pitfalls: Eisenhower Matrix
Daily To-Do List / Written Schedule
nodes.body: Stage 1 — Draft. A baseline organization habit: write a list of tasks for the day on a notepad. Used by Deborah daily; first lightly recommended to Jolene on 2023-03-02 ('break it into smaller pieces and set goals for yourself ... planners or schedulers help you stay organized'), then formally taught with detailed steps and pitfalls on 2023-03-22. Pitfall surfaced 2023-03-22: a long unprioritized list can feel overwhelming and stall progress, which is why Deborah pairs to-do lists with the Eisenhower Matrix.

nodes.header: Pitfalls: Daily To-Do List / Written Schedule
Steps: Choose one task to focus on for the next interval
nodes.body: Pick a single task to work on. Pomodoro is a single-tasking method — multitasking during the work interval defeats the purpose.

nodes.header: Steps: Set a timer for 25 minutes (one Pomodoro)
nodes.body: Use any timer. The fixed-duration interval is what creates the focus boundary. 25 minutes is the canonical Pomodoro length and the one Jolene uses.

nodes.header: Steps: Work without interruption until the timer rings
nodes.body: No context-switching, no checking phone, no other tasks. If a distracting thought arises, write it down to handle later and return to the task.

nodes.header: Steps: Take a 5-minute break, then repeat
nodes.body: Step away from the work — stand, stretch, look outside. The break is non-negotiable; skipping it is what causes the burnout the technique is designed to prevent. Then start a new Pomodoro.

nodes.header: Steps: Draw a 2x2 grid with urgency and importance as axes
nodes.body: One axis is urgency (urgent vs. not urgent), the other is importance (important vs. not important). The grid yields four quadrants. Visualizing the grid is part of how Deborah teaches it — she shared a visual breakdown to Jolene on 2023-03-22.

nodes.header: Steps: List every task currently on your plate
nodes.body: Capture every outstanding task before sorting. Sorting works only if the input is complete — missing tasks lead to rework.

nodes.header: Steps: Sort each task into one of the four quadrants by urgency and importance
nodes.body: Quadrant assignments: (1) Urgent + Important = do now, (2) Important + Not Urgent = schedule, (3) Urgent + Not Important = delegate if possible, (4) Neither = drop. The act of categorizing is what produces the focus, since it forces you to confront what truly matters versus what merely feels loud.

nodes.header: Steps: Work the quadrants in priority order — urgent+important first, then important+not urgent
nodes.body: Execute on the matrix. Quadrant 1 (urgent + important) gets immediate attention, then quadrant 2 (important + not urgent) is the strategic work. Quadrants 3 and 4 are minimized or dropped. Deborah described this as the way the matrix 'helps me figure out what's important and urgent so I'm more organized.'

nodes.header: Steps: Write all of today's tasks on a notepad at the start of the day
nodes.body: Deborah's habit: take a physical notepad and list everything that needs to be done today. Keeps the list in front of you all day.

nodes.header: Steps: Break large items down into smaller, concrete tasks
nodes.body: When Jolene felt overwhelmed by a 'big stack of tasks,' Deborah's coaching response was 'Have you tried breaking it down or prioritizing the tasks?' Decomposition is the first lever before prioritization.

nodes.header: Steps: Prioritize the list — pair with Eisenhower Matrix when the list is long
nodes.body: An unprioritized list of any size produces overwhelm. Deborah's escalation path is to pair the to-do list with the Eisenhower Matrix when it's heavy: list first, then sort by urgency and importance.

nodes.header: Steps: Work the list and check items off as you complete them
nodes.body: Execute top-down through the prioritized list, checking off completed items. Visible progress on the page helps reduce overwhelm.

nodes.header: Long unprioritized list feels overwhelming and stalls action — break tasks down and pair with Eisenhower Matrix
nodes.body: Symptoms: list grows long, user can't decide where to start, motivation drops. Root cause: a flat to-do list does not encode priority, so every task feels equally pressing. Fix: at step 2, decompose any large/abstract task into smaller concrete actions; at step 3, run the items through the Eisenhower Matrix to assign urgency/importance. Witnessed: Jolene experienced this exact failure mode on 2023-03-22 (her last-Friday notepad), which is what prompted Deborah to introduce the Eisenhower Matrix. Conversation: conv-48_session_10.

nodes.header: Pitfalls: Mindful Breathing for Yoga / Calming the Mind
Steps: Set aside a few minutes each day for the practice
nodes.body: Deborah's instruction (2023-06-06): 'Set aside a few minutes each day to sit with your eyes closed.' The practice is meant to be daily and brief — even a few minutes is enough. Establishing a daily cadence matters more than the duration of any single session.

nodes.header: Steps: Sit with eyes closed
nodes.body: Sit in a comfortable seated position with your eyes closed. The closed eyes remove visual distractions so you can direct your attention inward to the breath.

nodes.header: Steps: Take deep breaths
nodes.body: Take slow, deep breaths. Deep breathing is the active component of the practice — it physiologically calms the nervous system and gives the mind something concrete to attend to.

nodes.header: Steps: Focus on how the air feels entering and leaving your body
nodes.body: Direct attention to the physical sensation of the air moving in and out — the feel at the nostrils, the chest rising and falling. This is the mindfulness anchor: when the mind wanders, return to the sensation. Deborah described this as 'focus on how the air feels entering and leaving your body.'
